P1.evidence: The only proper setter read-back in this batch, and it was done exactly as the script intends: 'I know you spoke with Kim. He gave me like a head start on you. I want to kind of repeat it back, make sure nothing got left in translation. Please let me know if anything's incorrect as well. So what I've got here, ex-athlete, motocross, grappling, BJJ, coaching as well... Goal is to get leaner, midsection, get some muscle back, improve strength, mobility.' It made the prospect feel seen and it surfaced the head injury. Frame still two-part and agreement still a token, but P1 was run better here than anywhere else in the batch.

P2.evidence: Diet and training week both properly elicited — 'talk to me about your diet and your training' and 'Are you kind of back into training now?' — and the diet question used the setter's gluten-free note well. Age and height never established; weight only emerged inside the goal discussion. Work was asked, but at 00:30, after the money objection, and the purpose was the tax angle rather than qualification. Health conditions scored partial because the rep did raise the setter's flag — 'apparently you've had some illness or something, but we can touch on all that' — and then never touched on it: the head-injury history was answered with 'I'm glad you're feeling good' and dropped. No injury, pain or limitation question followed, so P2d is a miss on a prospect whose training history ended because of head trauma.

P3.evidence: The reflect-back was the best in the batch and it did real work: 'It sounds like really the goal here is to kind of get your mojo back... it also sounds like at the same time, you've almost, I wouldn't say fell out of love with training... Is that accurate or am I way off?' The prospect confirmed it and then explained the whole gym story. Return to grappling was picked up from the setter's notes. But the ladder stopped there — no bridge question, no 'what does that do for you', no 'who else does that impact'. A man mid-divorce, with a daughter, who lost his sport and his gym in the same season, and nothing beyond the physical was ever asked.

P4.evidence: P4e ran well through a smart two-example question — 'some people say I just need somebody to teach me how to use this stuff... other people say I need someone to wake me up in the morning. I guess for you, what would that be?' — and the prospect named his gap precisely: 'I don't think I need a whole lot of accountability... just learning the motions' and a small set of exercises, not 800. The mojo reflection also drew out why training stopped. But 'what have you tried before' was never asked, 'what's the one thing actually getting in the way' was never asked, and the root-cause question never ran. The excuse pattern he volunteered — 'it's always been something' — was left un-mined.

P5.evidence: Absent, and the omission is expensive here. This prospect had already told the rep he has been inactive for a year, that the reasons rotate, that he fell out of love with training and that he watches classes thinking 'it's probably easier being there doing the work than it is sitting here thinking about it'. That is a man one question away from articulating the cost of another year. No two-year question, no 'are you willing to settle for that', no line in the sand — so when $6,000 landed there was nothing on the other side of the scale.

P6.evidence: No commitment check of any kind. The rep moved from 'Any questions on any of that?' straight to next steps and the number. Neither the belief question nor the all-in question was asked, so when hesitation surfaced there was no established yes to return to — and the playbook's instruction to go back to Phase 5 on hesitation was unavailable, because Phase 5 had never happened.

P11.evidence: Nothing collected and no deposit offered, despite the rep using a $100 refundable deposit to hold follow-ups twice earlier in the same week. Onboarding slots were named ('a couple of times tomorrow morning and the next one would be Monday') and the prospect wanted the next day, but nothing was booked because the process requires payment first — confirmed on the call: 'I would assume we got to make the commitment and the payment before I talk to Trevor, right?' / 'That's right, yeah.' No agreement, no welcome email, no Skool link, no questionnaire.

objection_plays.detail: The best single move of the play ran — a clean isolate of the mechanism: 'Is it the like upfront amount that's concerning? It's like it's 6k upfront or what's the logistical concern for you?' That produced a real answer. But nothing else did. No 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place', no permission for an open financial conversation, and not one of the six FINANCIAL PICTURE questions — no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no credit cards, no available credit, no investments. The prospect volunteered the shape of his finances anyway (divorce, two households, lumpy contractor income), and the rep's response was to manufacture cheaper products rather than to map what he could actually afford. That is the inverse of what OC exists to do.

Timing was explicitly part of the blocker — 'some months are good and it's not an issue, and some months you're like oh how am I gonna make all this work' and 'I recently just restarted my business'. No OD move ran. Nothing on 'things never slow down', nothing on 'when does it actually become the right time', nothing on the cost of waiting. The rep instead accepted the timing frame and built a product around it.

'Let me do a little forecasting and see where things are' is the trigger. No move ran; the rep went straight to channel logistics and agreed to wait until morning. To his credit he asked a clean expectation-setting question — 'would you get back to me within the next three hours or would it be tomorrow?' — but that is call management, not the play.
No partner gate — the prospect is mid-divorce and the financial obligation to another household was raised as a constraint on him, not as a decision he shares.
No fear or doubt about the method; he was convinced by the technique-first argument and said 'A hundred percent'.

Script gap worth logging separately from the money play. This prospect may genuinely not be able to afford the offer — a divorce, two dependants' worth of outgoings and a business restarted weeks ago is a different situation from a wallet that needs opening, and OC assumes the latter. There is no scripted path for 'this person is a good fit and cannot currently pay', which is why the rep improvised three new price points in ten minutes. A disqualify-with-dignity move, or a legitimate low-tier product, is missing from the script.

notes: Best-run opening in the batch — the setter read-back is exactly right and the mojo reflect-back is genuinely skilled — attached to no Phase 5, no Phase 6 and a price that fell from $6,000 to $1,200 in four minutes on hesitation alone. Two coaching points, in order. When a prospect says his head injuries came back from loading his neck, that is a stop-and-screen, not a 'glad you're feeling good'. And when money surfaces, run the financial picture and find out what he can actually pay before inventing a tier that is not on the price list.
